name: PointCast · Nature
description: El Segundo field guide: local flora, dune habitat, and the El Segundo blue butterfly.

overview.title: El Segundo nature overview
overview.description: A high-level read of the local nature register: ocean, flora, trees, and wildlife before the detailed dune field guide.

areas.label: Ocean
areas.title: Pacific shoreline
areas.summary: The west edge is surf, marine layer, salt air, beach sand, and nearshore birds. It sets the weather and the tempo for the whole local nature register.

areas.label: Flora
areas.title: Dune plants
areas.summary: Seacliff buckwheat, beach suncups, deerweed, coyote brush, and other coastal scrub plants make El Segundo nature legible close to the ground.

areas.label: Trees
areas.title: Wind-shaped canopy
areas.summary: The exposed dune edge is more scrub than woodland, while streets, parks, and yards carry shade, nesting structure, and human-scale refuge.

areas.label: Wildlife
areas.title: Small but active
areas.summary: The signature species is the endangered El Segundo blue butterfly, with shorebirds, seabirds, lizards, pollinators, and occasional marine mammals in the broader coastal pass.

valueYieldSystem.description: Turn the El Segundo native planting palette from Block 0331 into an interactive site-fit, value-score, and establishment planner.

sourceBlock.title: Native planting palette for El Segundo

notes.name: Seacliff buckwheat
notes.signal: Cream-pink flowerheads on sandy bluffs and restored dunes.
notes.localRead: The anchor plant: El Segundo blue larvae feed in buckwheat flowerheads, so more buckwheat means more possible butterfly.

notes.name: El Segundo blue
notes.signal: Small blue butterflies moving low over buckwheat, mostly in protected dune habitat.
notes.localRead: The town-name species. Treat it like a broadcast from the dunes: watch from paths, leave habitat alone.

notes.name: Beach suncups
notes.signal: Low yellow flowers tucked into open sand.
notes.localRead: A small dune flash: the kind of plant you miss if you scan for trees instead of reading the ground.

notes.name: Deerweed
notes.signal: Fine green stems, yellow pea flowers, seed pods later.
notes.localRead: Restoration workhorse. It reads humble, but it helps rebuild a plant community in tired sand.

notes.name: Coyote brush
notes.signal: Rounded coastal scrub, evergreen mass, pale seed fluff when it goes.
notes.localRead: The background note of coastal scrub: shelter, pollen, edge habitat, and wind-proof structure.

notes.name: LAX dunes
notes.signal: One of the last big fragments of the old coastal dune system beside the runways.
notes.localRead: El Segundo nature is not wilderness over there; it is a protected remnant, still speaking through sand, buckwheat, and repair.

plantingPalette.name: Seacliff buckwheat
plantingPalette.place: Sunny coastal edge, sandy strip, or dry front yard.
plantingPalette.why: Pollinator magnet and the strongest symbolic link to the El Segundo blue.
plantingPalette.caution: Best treated as habitat planting, not a clipped ornamental.

plantingPalette.name: Beach suncups
plantingPalette.place: Open sandy pocket, parkway edge, or low pot with fast drainage.
plantingPalette.why: Low yellow bloom that keeps the dune register close to the ground.

plantingPalette.name: Deerweed
plantingPalette.place: Dry slope, sandy border, or restoration patch that can look loose.
plantingPalette.why: Fast, useful structure for rebuilding poor soil and feeding insects.

plantingPalette.name: Coyote brush
plantingPalette.place: Wind-facing hedge, slope, or rear edge where structure matters.
plantingPalette.why: Evergreen mass, late-season pollen, and shelter for small wildlife.
plantingPalette.caution: Give it room or choose a prostrate form for smaller spaces.

plantingPalette.name: Lemonade berry
plantingPalette.place: Larger yard edge, privacy screen, or coastal slope.
plantingPalette.why: Classic coastal scrub mass: glossy leaves, flowers, berries, bird value.
plantingPalette.caution: Too large for most balcony containers.

plantingPalette.name: Coast sunflower
plantingPalette.place: Sunny dry bed where a bright, informal bloom is welcome.
plantingPalette.why: South Coast scrub signal: yellow flowers, pollinator traffic, easy visual read.

nativePlantingYield.title: Block 0331 native planting value system
nativePlantingYield.yieldDefinition: Value yield means local habitat signal, water fit, repeatable action, and legible public learning. It is not an investment or financial return.
nativePlantingYield.operatingPrinciple: Turn one short block into an installable palette, a 90-day care loop, and a machine-readable plan that another human or agent can reuse.

metrics.label: Habitat lift
metrics.signal: native flowers, shelter, seedheads, and insect traffic
metrics.measure: Count how many palette species survive to second bloom.

metrics.label: Water fit
metrics.signal: rain-season establishment with lower dry-season demand
metrics.measure: Track weeks watered after establishment, then reduce when roots hold.

metrics.label: Local literacy
metrics.signal: neighbors can name buckwheat, suncups, deerweed, and scrub
metrics.measure: A plant label, a block link, or one shared cutting/seed note.

metrics.label: Repeatability
metrics.signal: balcony, parkway, and yard versions all use the same grammar
metrics.measure: Document the site type, plant mix, and what changed after 90 days.

operatingRules: Match plants to sun, drainage, mature size, and foot traffic before buying anything.
Plant during the cool rainy season when possible; use the first dry season as establishment, not performance.
Leave some seedheads and imperfect structure so the garden can work as habitat.
Avoid invasive groundcovers, especially iceplant near dune-adjacent places.

phases.label: Read
phases.action: Map sun, drainage, wind, container depth, and where people walk.

phases.label: Plant
phases.action: Install the smallest useful mix and water deeply through establishment.

phases.label: Watch
phases.action: Log bloom, insect traffic, leaf stress, and irrigation changes for 90 days.

phases.label: Share
phases.action: Publish the mix, misses, and one photo back to the block or local channel.

sitePlans.name: Balcony tray
sitePlans.siteRead: Windy, bright, shallow, and fully visible. Keep the mix low and tough.
sitePlans.value: A tiny public-facing native signal that teaches the palette without pretending to be dune restoration.
sitePlans.water: Hand-water through the first dry season; use fast drainage and do not let pots sit in runoff.
nextMoves: Choose containers with drainage holes and enough weight for coastal wind.
Top-dress with mineral mulch; skip rich, wet potting mixes.
Photo-log bloom and leaf stress once a week for 90 days.

sitePlans.name: Parkway strip
sitePlans.siteRead: Hot, walked-by, compacted at the edges, and easy to over-tidy.
sitePlans.value: Turns a dead strip into a low-water learning strip with flowers, structure, and visible seasonal change.
sitePlans.water: Deep establishment water beats frequent sprinkles; keep water off sidewalks.
nextMoves: Check city parkway rules and keep sightlines clear.
Break compaction gently and avoid imported high-fertility soil.
Mulch around starts, not over crowns, and leave a walking edge.

sitePlans.name: Front yard patch
sitePlans.siteRead: Enough room for layers: low flowers, loose repair plants, and evergreen coastal scrub.
sitePlans.value: Creates a durable local habitat patch that can replace thirsty ornamental area over time.
sitePlans.water: Rain-season planting plus monthly deep checks during the first dry season.
nextMoves: Place shrubs first by mature size, then fill between them with lower plants.
Group plants by water need so establishment does not punish the dry-adapted ones.
Remove invasive groundcover in phases so bare soil is not left open too long.

sitePlans.name: Wild edge
sitePlans.siteRead: A larger slope, fence line, or back edge that can look wilder and carry real structure.
sitePlans.value: Builds a recognizable coastal scrub edge: shelter, flowers, berries, and seasonal roughness.
sitePlans.water: Establish with deep infrequent water, then let dry-season structure be part of the look.

mix.role: large coastal mass and bird value

nextMoves: Mark paths before planting so habitat does not get stepped through.
Plant larger shrubs with their mature width in mind, not nursery size.
Keep a simple quarterly log: bloom, seed, bird/insect activity, water used.

seasonalSignals.read: Cool-season rain wakes roots before the visible show.
seasonalSignals.fieldNote: Planting and light establishment work belong here when rain is helping.

seasonalSignals.read: Deerweed, suncups, and scrub flowers start making the ground legible.
seasonalSignals.fieldNote: Watch for yellow first, then seed pods and insect traffic.

seasonalSignals.read: Seacliff buckwheat becomes the headline; El Segundo blue flight season sits close to it.
seasonalSignals.fieldNote: Stay on paths near dune habitat. Small movement matters.

seasonalSignals.read: Flower color drops; seedheads, coyote brush, and wind-shaped forms carry the page.
seasonalSignals.fieldNote: This is when the scrub looks quiet but still holds shelter and food.

transect.label: Sand
transect.signal: Open dune, beach suncups, wind, sparse growth.

transect.label: Buckwheat
transect.signal: Seacliff buckwheat anchors the butterfly story.

transect.label: Scrub
transect.signal: Coyote brush and deerweed hold structure.

transect.label: Town
transect.signal: Balconies, yards, parks, and tiny native patches.

fieldRules: Stay on paths around protected dune habitat.
Plant climate-matched California natives where possible.
Notice small seasonal signals: flowerheads, seed pods, wind shadow, and return.
